prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

On the day I set out on the climb, grief saddled in my back like a bag of marbles, my breath like clouds hanging on the low peaks of a mountain, on the day I set out leaving nothing behind, nothing on the bed, no version of myself, just my voice through the night, the voice I use to ward off nightmares. (My voice is a still life in itself, a shroud green and ultramarine deep blue, a bowl of apples and tangerines on a table.) On the day I set out, the mountain is high in front of me, the unreliable god of mist and fog. I have no voice to say how high my fingers must lift as if on a lover's upper lip, to take in the breath of how high my mountain is—white teeth behind a snow cap, numberless springs, cold like the enzymes in spit— a version of me is still asleep: the moving of a limb in sleep. Everything becomes lucid.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Everything

outputs.L1: On the day I set out to climb, grief saddled on my back like a bag of marbles, my breath like clouds hanging over the low peaks of a mountain. On the day I set out, I left nothing behind—nothing on the bed, no version of myself—only my voice passing through the night, the voice I use to ward off nightmares. (My voice is a still life unto itself: a shroud of green and deep ultramarine blue, a bowl of apples and tangerines on a table.) On the day I set out, the mountain rises high before me, an unreliable god of mist and fog. I have no voice with which to say how high my fingers must lift, as though brushing a lover’s upper lip, to draw in the breath of how high my mountain is—white teeth behind a snowcap, numberless springs, cold as the enzymes in spit. A version of me is still asleep: the movement of a limb in sleep. Everything becomes lucid.
outputs.L2: The morning I began my ascent, sorrow rattled inside my spine like a pouch filled with glass beads, and each exhale hovered like vapor around a mountain’s lower ridges. I departed without leaving anything behind—not an impression in the sheets, not another self—only my voice traveling through the darkness, the sound I summon to keep bad dreams away. (That voice is its own painted arrangement: a cloth of shroud-green and fathomless ultramarine, with apples and tangerines gathered in a bowl upon a table.) When I started out, the mountain towered before me, a fickle deity made of haze and cloud. Words failed me; I could not describe how far my fingers would have to rise, touching the height as delicately as a lover’s upper lip, nor could I breathe in the full scale of the peak—its snowy crown concealing white teeth, its countless springs chilled like the enzymes in saliva. Somewhere, another me remained asleep, no more than an arm or leg shifting in a dream. Then everything sharpened into clarity.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins a difficult ascent while carrying the immense weight of grief. As they leave the past behind, they abandon every former version of themself, preserving only a single voice—the voice once used to keep nightmares at bay. In their imagination, this voice becomes a vivid still life, rich with deep colors and abundant fruit, suggesting that it remains alive with beauty and creative power despite their sorrow.

Ahead, the mountain rises as an immense and mysterious presence. Shrouded in mist, fog, and snow, it appears unstable and difficult to trust, reflecting the speaker’s uncertainty about the journey to come. As the climb begins, the speaker feels divided: one part of them remains metaphorically asleep, still bound to grief and the past, while the surrounding world sharpens into sudden clarity. This contrast captures a moment of transition in which the speaker moves forward physically, even though some part of the self has not yet fully awakened.
outputs.L4:
The speaker confronts grief as though undertaking a difficult ascent up a mountain. Each step becomes an act of endurance, and the surrounding landscape reflects the speaker’s inner struggle: the steep slopes suggest the weight of sorrow, while the thin air evokes breathlessness, exhaustion, and the effort required simply to continue. Images of breath and voice emphasize the tension between silence and expression. Grief threatens to take away the speaker’s ability to speak, yet the climb gradually restores a sense of presence, as if naming or inhabiting pain makes it possible to breathe again.

Sleep functions as another important metaphor. It represents numbness, withdrawal, and the former self that existed before grief was fully confronted. As the speaker climbs, the world suddenly sharpens into focus. This moment of lucidity feels like an awakening: the landscape becomes clearer, the body more alert, and the speaker more conscious of both loss and survival. Yet the transformation is incomplete. An older version of the self remains behind, suspended in sleep, unable or unwilling to awaken. The ascent therefore does not erase grief or restore the speaker to who they once were. Instead, it reveals that mourning creates a divided identity—one self moves forward with painful clarity, while another remains fixed in the past. By turning grief into a mountain climb, the text portrays sorrow as both an ordeal and a form of awakening, suggesting that facing loss can bring the self back to life even as part of it remains forever attached to what has been lost.
outputs.L5:
## Everything

Everything begins with almost nothing: a breath, a spark, a question.

From that small beginning, the world unfolds—oceans and cities, memories and possibilities, ordinary mornings and life-changing nights. Everything includes what we understand and what remains mysterious. It is the warmth of sunlight on a window, the silence between two people, the distant movement of galaxies, and the private hope that tomorrow might be different.

Yet no one can hold everything at once. We experience life in fragments: one conversation, one choice, one fleeting moment after another. Perhaps that is why small things matter so much. A kind word can become someone’s courage. A mistake can become wisdom. A simple decision can redirect an entire life.

Everything is connected, even when the connections are invisible. The past shapes the present; the present opens the future. What we give returns in unexpected forms. What we ignore may continue to grow. Each person carries a universe of thoughts, fears, dreams, and untold stories.

To think about everything is to face both wonder and uncertainty. It reminds us how little we control, but also how much we can influence. We may never understand the whole, yet we can still choose how to meet our part of it—with curiosity, compassion, and attention.

In the end, everything may be too vast to explain. But perhaps it is not meant to be explained all at once. Perhaps everything is meant to be lived, one meaningful moment at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about climbing a mountain while carrying grief, using surreal imagery, repetition, and long flowing sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
I climbed because the mountain had entered me, because its black pines were already growing through my ribs, because somewhere above the clouds the snow kept repeating your name in a language made only of silence and light.

I carried grief in a blue bowl balanced against my heart, and though the bowl had no weight, my knees bent beneath it, my breath came loose in silver animals, my shadow dragged behind me like a drowned dress filled with stones.

Still, I climbed.

Past the village where every window dreamed of fire, past the field where the moon lay broken among the sheep, past the river turning its long glass key in the lock of the earth, I climbed, and with every step the path unstitched itself behind me, leaving no road home, no road home, no road home.

At dawn, the clouds descended and placed their pale hands over my eyes, and I walked blind through a forest of antlers, hearing your laughter fall from branch to branch, hearing it become rain, hearing the rain become small white moths that gathered in my mouth whenever I tried to speak.

Still, I climbed.

Grief changed shape as the air thinned: first a child asleep on my back, then a bell without a tongue, then a door I carried through every doorless place, and sometimes it was only your absence, vast and ordinary, sitting beside me on a stone as we shared the last red apple in the world.

The mountain grew taller whenever I remembered you, its summit lifting like a ship into the stars, its glaciers opening their blue eyes, its cliffs murmuring, Not yet, not yet, not yet, while far below the valleys folded themselves into green letters I could no longer read.

I climbed until my hands became roots, until my blood filled with migrating birds, until the sun was a golden wound stitched to the sky, and all the while I spoke to you—not with words, but with breath, with bone, with the small stubborn thunder of my feet.

Still, I climbed.

Near the summit, night came suddenly, pouring from a cracked cup, and the stars hung so low they caught in my hair; I saw the dead walking quietly across the snow, each carrying a lantern made from something they had loved, and you were among them, or you were the light, or you were the snow receiving every footprint and keeping none.

Then grief leaned close and whispered that it had never been a burden, not entirely, but a rope tied between my living body and the vanished world, a dark rope, a bright rope, a rope I had mistaken for chains.

At last I reached the place where the mountain ended and the sky began, though there was no summit, only wind, only whiteness, only the whole earth turning below me like a sleeping blue animal, and I opened my hands to set grief down.

But grief rose.

It rose from the bowl in a flock of blue wings, it rose through my ribs and carried the pines with it, it rose until the heavens were crowded with impossible birds, and for one breath, one endless breath, your absence became not emptiness but distance, not silence but a song too large for any single mouth.

And I stood there, lighter but not light, broken but not falling, while the mountain breathed beneath me and the snow went on repeating your name, your name, your name, until it sounded almost like mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person paragraph beginning with “On the day I set out,” in which a mountain journey becomes a metaphor for loss and self-transformation.
counterfactuals.output: On the day I set out, the mountain wore the face of everyone I had lost: clouded brow, granite mouth, snow closing over the eyes. I climbed as if altitude could translate absence, each switchback turning grief into a new grammar—stone, breath, silence; stone, breath, silence—until the trail thinned and even my name felt too heavy to carry. Behind me, the valley folded shut like an old letter. Ahead, the summit kept receding, a white erasure. Somewhere above the tree line I understood that I had mistaken arrival for healing, that the mountain was not asking me to conquer it but to shed, layer by layer, the person who had begun. So I left my sorrow in cairns along the ridge—not gone, never gone, but rearranged—and descended at dusk with different weather under my skin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue about leaving one’s former self behind to ascend a mist-covered mountain. Include images of breath, sleep, voice, fruit, snow, and the body.
counterfactuals.output:
I left my former self beside the road,  
still wearing my name like a weathered coat.  
It did not call after me.  
Perhaps it had already fallen asleep,  
its hands folded over the old hungers  
of the body.

Above, the mountain vanished into mist.  
Each step erased the path below;  
each breath became a pale animal  
leaving me for the cold.

I climbed until my voice grew strange—  
not mine, not anyone’s—  
a small bell sounding under snow.  
The silence answered  
by opening its white mouth.

At the tree line, I found one fruit  
clinging to a black branch,  
red as a last wound,  
sweet as what cannot be carried.  
I ate it whole: seed, sorrow, winter.

Then sleep rose from the valleys  
and covered the world I had been.  
My body, weary and bright with frost,  
no longer seemed a prison,  
but a door standing open.

I crossed through.

At the summit there was no crown,  
no god, no final word—  
only snow falling through my breath,  
only mist lifting from the stone,  
and far below, beside the empty road,  
the self I had abandoned  
softening into earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike prose poem in the style of contemporary literary poetry, blending grief, landscape, intimacy, and still-life imagery. End with the sentence “Everything becomes lucid.”
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, the hills loosen their dark hair into the river. I carry your absence in a blue bowl, careful not to spill it, though it has no weight and no edge. In the kitchen, pears soften beside a small brass key; dust settles on the cups we once lifted to each other’s mouths. Outside, rain rehearses its silver alphabet against the windows.

I dream you are sleeping beneath the orchard, your hands folded around a green apple. Roots pass gently through your sleeves. When I call your name, the deer raise their heads, each face briefly yours, then vanish into the wet ferns. The path continues without us, pale with stones and fallen blossoms.

By morning, the room is full of ordinary mercies: a knife, a linen cloth, three plums bruised purple in a dish. I touch the hollow your body left in the mattress and feel the whole valley breathing there—the lake holding its cold mirror, the reeds bowing, the clouds opening their white doors.

Nothing returns, yet everything leans closer: the salt cellar, the chair, the photograph turned toward the wall. Grief ripens quietly among them, a dark fruit we divide with our bare hands. I taste rain, iron, your vanished mouth. Beyond the glass, sunlight enters the field and rests on every blade of grass.

Everything becomes lucid.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the start of a difficult mountain climb from the perspective of a grieving speaker, using anaphora, parenthetical asides, synesthesia, unexpected similes, and ambiguous punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
I begin before dawn, when the mountain is still withholding its face.

I begin with your gloves in my pack (though they do not fit me).  
I begin with the rope whispering blue against the ice.  
I begin because standing still has become another way of falling.

At the trailhead, snow tastes like a struck bell. The pines crowd close, black and solemn as drowned ladders, and my breath climbs ahead of me—small ghost, impatient guide. Somewhere above, the summit sharpens the dark.

You would have laughed at the weather (you laughed at worse things). You would have called this wind *bracing*, this slope *honest*. I call them by no name; names are doors and I have closed enough—

The first step sinks to the ankle.  
The second finds stone.  
The third—

is that where the climb begins, or where I leave you?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
